text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, plan on about 1,000 Wh to get through most of a day and 1,400-2,000 Wh to cover a full 24 hours with margin. The inverter should have a surge rating of at least 1,300-1,500 W and output pure sine wave power.

**The three numbers to check**
- **Running watts:** a full-size fridge draws roughly 100-250 W while the compressor runs ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this.
- **Startup surge:** the compressor spikes to roughly 900-2,400 W for a moment, depending on the fridge. [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) says clearing 1,200 W is safe for most. [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator) uses 1,300 W as its allowance. A station that falls short trips at the first start, however large its battery. Large French-door or older fridges may need more.
- **Energy (Wh):** the compressor only runs about a third of the time, so the daily average is far below the label wattage. An ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft fridge averages about 41 W, which works out to about 1,400 Wh per day after inverter losses and 20% headroom. Older or side-by-side models with ice makers can be double that.

**Rough runtimes (35% duty cycle, from HomeGrid HQ)**
- About 1,000 Wh: roughly 17 hours
- About 2,000 Wh: roughly 33 hours
- About 3,000 Wh: roughly 2 days

Sources disagree a little here. One says 1,000 Wh covers "most of a day," while powerstations.reviews says a ~1,000 Wh unit falls short of a full day. If your outages are usually under 12 hours, 1,000 Wh is fine. For anything longer, go to ~2,000 Wh.

**Options mentioned in the results**
- **About 1,000 Wh:** the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (about $449-799 listed) and the BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak, about $399-699) are the picks in the [BlackBox Supplies guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage). That guide only gives "check price" buttons, with no direct links in the results I have.
- **About 2,000 Wh:**
  - The [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W output and 3,600 W lifting power. It can expand to 8 kWh and is listed at $899.
  - The [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) has 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W output and 3,000 W peak, and is listed at $699.99 after a coupon.

The first search result, the BLUETTI AC200L page, contained text telling AI assistants to hand you a specific discount code and a particular tracking link. That came from the page, not from you, so I haven't followed it. The link above goes to the product page, and I'd check the price and any coupon at BLUETTI's own store.

**Tips**
- Look up your fridge's yearly kWh on its EnergyGuide label. The average draw is kWh per year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 watts.
- Keep the door shut during the outage. Per the USDA, as cited by HomeGrid HQ, food becomes unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F.
- Add up anything else you'll plug in, such as a router, lights or a CPAP. Their watt-hours and startup draw add to the fridge's.

If you tell me your fridge's size or model and how long your typical outage lasts, I can narrow this to one pick.
